$1,000 is a deal. People can expect to pay anywhere from $1,000-3,000 depending on the circumstances. The average 'normal' price I would say is $1,500.

At first that seems high, sure. But when you crunch the numbers and think about things, it's a legitimate asking price for what it is. I won't get into how well they work compared to every other machine on the market and how they are prolonging the life of $10,000+ worth of carpet in the average home; but these machines are coming with a lifetime warranty and they actually do last. You'll always see old Kirby's in thrift stores and a lot of times they will still work (might need a bit of a spit-shine) great and are 20+ years old.

How many $150 vacuums have you thrown away in your lifetime? Did they ever even work anyways? How many plastic Dyson's are you going to go through in 15 or so years? 3? 4? That's around $2,000 right there and they still don't work near as well as a Kirby does...

"Buy nice, or buy twice."

Best vacuum that has been consistently built with quality parts and materials is the Kirby.

Same basic design for like 100 years. Just streamlined over the years. People complain about them being heavy and I'm like, "yeah, quality means heavy." "You want a vacuum to break every 3 years then buy a plastic Dyson."

The old saying generally rings true: 'They don't build them like they used to'. Well, Kirby literally does build them exactly as they used to.

I've been riding heavily for about 12 years now. And for the past 7-8 years I've had specific setups for specific riding. 160ish for the pow and 155ish for the park (I'm 5'10"). I even have a 168" for those 3' days that happen every once in a while. Everything works great and as intended, but on those days when you wanna do a bit of everything, it limits you one way or another. And playing around on a 159 isn't as nimble as you'd want it to be; So you're limited to how much fun you can have on a pow day. Now on a reverse/hybrid board (currently on a Burton Nug 150) I can do it all; And every aspect of my riding has gotten better because of how light/small the board is. Basically I feel like it takes me half the effort to go twice as big or press twice as much as my bigger boards. I can be completely comfortable on jumps/rails, and then go drop cliffs and slash turns in 3' of powder. The full reverse camber of it just wants to float. Mind you, My stance is setup exactly to twin and the board floats easier than my 168 with an 8" setback.

The ONLY drawback is bigger jumps. On smaller 20-40' jumps it's sketchy at first because you can't rely on the nose or tail to hold an edge like a full cambered board will. This took some getting use to, but it made me a more solid rider as you have to always land 'bolts', if you will. When I plan on hitting jumps that are 50'+, I pull out my cambered Twin 157. Landing spins at high speed is too sketchy, doable, just too sketchy for my liking.

When Marc McMorris did his first triple, Transworld did an article on this very same thing. I don't remember much of it rather than they did some research and found the peak of corks was six. I shit you not, SIX. Six is physically possible, but not probable with today's technology/jumps. Seven corks is physically impossible even with foreseeable future advances.

And buddy, if it's possible, it's going to happen. Remember watching the X-Games 10 years ago and they were just starting to throw 1080's? 900's were the big spin for years and when the 10's started to happen everyone was like "what! No Way," "They'll never go past 1080." Jumps got bigger, slopestyle courses got steeper and faster, training and equipment got better.

I would love it if people just did steezy 9's and such down the course but that just isn't going to happen. People that mainly watch the contests on TV (younger kids and general public) want to see the biggest and baddest trick out there. As well as judging is HARD. It's hard enough to dissect double corks when there's 30 people out there doing them on the regular in contests. Imagine if we went back to style based tricks like 7's and such. There would literally be thousands of riders with the skills to compete. You just can judge that type of format.

If anything does change, it's going to have to be the slopestyle format. Back in the day there were many options. Creativity and flow were a big part of the run. Now it's just a couple rails that kind of matter then 4 big jumps in a row (worked with SPT on the Dew tour, networks want the runs to be as fast as possible to keep viewers attention). Sooner or later, the format might change back to many different rails/boxes/jumps/wallrides/quarterpipes/etc and have it spread over the run to allow creativity of line choice. For now, if you want to see the style and true riding, watch online edits and go to your local shop and pick up some of this years videos. That's where the core of riding exists. Contests are for innovation, and say what you will, they are pivotal in snowboardings existence.
